confirmed.claim: Canonical topology labels alone do NOT resolve symmetry-equivalent-but-distinct events: in symmetric configurations, distinct events can share identical initial/saddle/final topologies, the same barrier, and the same absolute displacement, so k-ART additionally encodes the direction of atomic motion to discriminate them, and validates on highly symmetric Si and Fe states that this recovers all pathways. This is direct evidence bearing on automorphism/symmetry handling in question (a).
confirmed.quote: In certain symmetric configurations, it is possible that distinct events associated with a given atom have identical topologies of initial state, saddle point, and final state, and the same barrier height and absolute displacement. To distinguish between those and fully account for the symmetries, we also include the direction of atomic motion in the description of events. Checks on a number of highly symmetric states in Si and Fe show that this classification recovers all pathways and accurately discriminates between them.

confirmed.claim: A graph canonization function C is DEFINED by two formal properties: C(G) is isomorphic to G, AND C(G^gamma)=C(G) for every relabeling gamma in S_n (order-independence / isomorphism invariance) - so all isomorphic graphs receive the SAME canonical representation regardless of input vertex ordering. This is precisely the guarantee an anchored point-group minimization with a frame-dependent tie-break lacks: a canonical form is invariant under all input permutations, not just a hand-chosen subgroup about one anchor.
confirmed.quote: A canonization algorithm can be seen as a function on graphs, C : G -> G, with the following properties, [15, C1 and C2]: C(G) ~= G and C(G^gamma) = C(G), for all gamma in Sn. That is, it returns a graph isomorphic to its input, and it is invariant with respect to permutations of its input. The second property is also called isomorphism invariance

confirmed.claim: The individualization-refinement paradigm (nauty/Traces) simultaneously computes both a canonical form and a generating set for the graph's automorphism group, so automorphism detection is a byproduct of canonical labeling rather than a separate procedure.
confirmed.quote: Traces computes a canonical form for a colored graph and/or a set of generators for its automorphism group.

confirmed.claim: All state-of-the-art practical graph canonization tools (nauty, Bliss, Traces) are built on one core method - the individualization-refinement paradigm: a tree search over successively refined vertex-set partitions - and they differ ONLY in heuristics for traversing/pruning the tree and refining partitions, not in the correctness of the resulting canonical form. Heuristic choices affect performance, not the guarantee.
confirmed.quote: They are all build on the same core idea of a tree search over gradually more refined partitions of the vertex set, also called the individualization-refinement paradigm. Their difference is thus essentially in the heuristics for traversing and pruning the search tree, and how partitions are being refined.

confirmed.claim: k-ART classifies each atom's local environment by building a truncated connectivity graph (bonds only, no geometry) and analyzing it with the graph-automorphism software NAUTY (McKay), which returns a canonical topology index plus the permutation key needed to reconstruct the geometry; this index is hashed to a unique topology label. This is the concrete production example of nauty-based canonical topology keys for chemistry/environment classification cited in research question (a).
confirmed.quote: This graph is then analyzed and classified using the freely available topological software NAUTY, developed by McKay [16]. This software package provides the topology index and all information necessary for uniquely identifying each environment, including the permutation key needed to reconstruct a specific geometry from the generic topology and a set of reference positions. The topology index from NAUTY has the form of an ordered set of three integers, which we use as input to a hash function to generate a unique topology label (hash key).

confirmed.claim: A canonical labeling provides a formal guarantee that two graphs are isomorphic if and only if their canonical forms are identical (equal), which is exactly the true-canonical-form property that an anchored point-group minimization lacks.
confirmed.quote: The image of a graph G under a function C : G → G is a canonical labeling (or canonical form) of G iff (i) ∀G ∈ G : C(G) ≃ G, (ii) ∀G1,G2 ∈ G : G1 ≃ G2 ⇔ C(G1) = C(G2).

confirmed.claim: The individualization-refinement approach computes the graph's automorphism group as a by-product of canonization and uses it to prune the search tree: when two distinct leaves produce representationally-equal permuted graphs (alpha=pi_{tau_a}, beta=pi_{tau_b}, G^alpha = G^beta), the composition alpha*beta^{-1} is an automorphism of G, and the complete automorphism group is obtained from all such leaf pairs. This supplies exactly the automorphism-order (symmetry number) that a hand-rolled anchored minimization does not expose.
confirmed.quote: One of the most successful tools is nauty [14], which not only finds a canonical representation but also computes the automorphism group, which during the canonization is used for pruning the search tree... with alpha = pi_{tau_a} and beta = pi_{tau_b} then G^alpha = G^beta. Permuting both sides with beta gives G^{alpha beta} = ... = G, meaning that alpha beta is an automorphism of G... the complete automorphism group can be computed by considering all such pairs of leaf nodes

confirmed.claim: Canonical labeling provides a strong guarantee that a hand-rolled anchored point-group minimization lacks: any two isomorphic labeled objects become bit-for-bit identical after canonical labeling, so a single equality test settles isomorphism (directly bears on RQ-a: the anchored D4h minimization is not a true canonical form because equivalent objects are not guaranteed to map to an identical representative).
confirmed.quote: Two labeled objects which are isomorphic become identical when they are canonically labeled.

confirmed.claim: The defining property (C2) is label-invariance: renaming the vertices of the input renames the output vertices identically, so the canonical output is independent of any labelling/frame choice -- the precise property violated by a frame-dependent, lexicographically-anchored tie-break, whose output changes when the input is relabelled.
confirmed.quote: Property (C2) is an important property that must be satisfied by many functions we define. It says that if the elements of V appearing in the inputs to the function are renamed in some manner, the elements of V appearing in the function value are renamed in the same manner. We call this label-invariance.

confirmed.claim: The topology-key scheme is only a valid canonical identity under an explicit precondition: the connectivity graph of local neighbors must map to a unique relaxed structure under the given interatomic potential (graph identity = configuration identity).
confirmed.quote: It is important that the configuration be uniquely defined through this network, i.e., the connectivity graph must lead to a unique structure once relaxed with a given interatomic potential.

confirmed.claim: k-ART resolves the multi-anchor ambiguity for multi-site events with a frame-independent physical rule — each event is anchored to the topology centered on the atom with the largest displacement, overriding whatever atom the trial search started from — rather than a lexicographic site tie-break.
confirmed.quote: To simplify labelling, each event is assigned to the topology centered on the atom that moved the most during the event, irrespective of the initial trial assignment.

confirmed.claim: k-ART's local-environment identity is computed by McKay's nauty canonical-labeling program, which guarantees a unique topology key per environment and also returns the permutation key needed to map the generic (canonical) topology onto a specific local geometry — i.e., canonical labeling supplies both collision-free identity and the group/permutation data a hand-rolled anchored point-group minimization lacks.
confirmed.quote: This classification is performed using the freely available topological software nauty, developed by McKay, which provides the topology index and all information necessary for uniquely identifying each environment, including the permutation key needed to reconstruct a specific geometry from the generic topology and a set of reference positions.

confirmed.claim: A canonical form C maps every coloured graph to a unique, label-invariant representative of its isomorphism class, giving the biconditional (G,pi) isomorphic to (G',pi') if and only if C(G,pi) = C(G',pi') -- exactly the guarantee an anchored point-group minimization lacks, so truly equivalent (symmetric) events must receive identical class ids instead of fragmenting across orientations.
confirmed.quote: A canonical form is a function C : G x Pi -> G x Pi such that, for all G, pi and g in Sn, (C1) C(G, pi) ~= (G, pi), (C2) C(G^g, pi^g) = C(G, pi). In other words, it assigns to each coloured graph an isomorphic coloured graph that is a unique representative of its isomorphism class. It follows from the definition that (G, pi) ~= (G', pi') <=> C(G, pi) = C(G', pi').

confirmed.claim: nauty/Traces obtain the canonical form via the individualization-refinement method (McKay-Piperno), which partitions vertices through sequential refinement steps — the specific technique the research question attributes to production canonical graph labeling.
confirmed.quote: The process of finding the canonical member of the isomorphism class containing a given object is called canonical labeling.

unverified.claim: The study computes, via first-principles DFT, migration barriers for a complete set of distinct surface and sub-surface vacancy migration paths near the FCC Ni-Cr (100) free surface — i.e., it treats near-surface hop barriers as path- and layer-resolved quantities rather than a single bulk value, which is the premise behind a layer-dependent (rather than global O_h vs D4h) catalogue symmetry.
unverified.quote: We survey a complete set of surface and sub-surface migration paths for vacancies near the (100) free surface and calculate the corresponding migration barriers.

unverified.claim: The Stamatakis-Vlachos framework identifies which events can fire by solving a subgraph isomorphism problem (implemented with Ullmann's algorithm) mapping each elementary-step pattern graph onto the lattice graph, with three matching conditions: edge (neighboring) preservation, site-type equality, and existence of an entity mapping whose coverage patterns match — i.e., event identity is established by graph matching against the live configuration, not by a hand-canonicalized geometric key.
unverified.quote: Having defined the elementary steps, the basic idea is then to solve a subgraph isomorphism problem for each elementary step defined, in order to identify the lattice processes that can take place.

unverified.claim: Zacros's graph-theoretical cluster-expansion Hamiltonian weights each energetic figure's contribution by an explicit graph multiplicity factor GM_gamma, which the authors identify as a symmetry number, multiplied against the count of lattice instances N_CE_gamma — i.e., the precise weighting rule that keeps total energy correct for patterns with internal symmetry is E contribution = ECI_gamma x GM_gamma x N_CE_gamma.
unverified.quote: where ECIγ is the effective cluster interaction for figure γ, GMγ is the graph multiplicity (essentially a symmetry number), and NCEγ is the number of instances of figure γ on the lattice

unverified.claim: EAM (Foiles-Baskes-Daw) static calculations give a surface-vacancy in-plane jump migration barrier of 0.47 eV on Cu(100), and the earlier literature value of 0.35 eV is explicitly identified as erroneous — establishing that the top-layer in-plane vacancy hop on an FCC(100) surface has a barrier well below the ~0.7 eV bulk Cu vacancy migration scale, i.e. near-surface vacancy barriers are layer-dependent.
unverified.quote: In Fig. 1, we show the mechanism by which a vacancy diffuses on the (100) surface — basically a jump. The corresponding barrier is 0.47 eV (cf. Table II), larger than the value of 0.35 eV reported in Ref. 36, which is in error.

unverified.claim: In dilute Ni-Cr, a vacancy migrating toward the (100) free surface has systematically lower barriers for exchange with a neighboring Cr atom than with a Ni atom, so near-surface hop rates are species-dependent (Ni-Cr-specific chemistry coloring of the event catalogue).
unverified.quote: A vacancy migrating towards the free surface will face lower energy barriers to migrate via atomic exchange with a neighboring Cr atom rather than with a Ni atom.

unverified.claim: Ab initio DFT-GGA gives a surface-vacancy diffusion barrier of 0.42 eV (error bar at most 20%) on Cu(100), in close agreement with the 0.47 eV EAM value and below the adatom jump barrier — providing first-principles corroboration that EAM captures the surface-layer vacancy hop barrier on FCC(100).
unverified.quote: The barrier for the diffusion of vacancies was also determined ab initio using the GGA. Its value, given in Table II along with other barriers, is estimated to be 0.42 eV, with an error bar of at most 20%. Again, the agreement with the EAM result, 0.47 eV, is striking.

unverified.claim: In this 2011 paper the weighting rule is one lattice process per subgraph-isomorphism mapping — every distinct mapping is enumerated as a separate process with its own propensity — and the paper contains no explicit division by the pattern graph's automorphism-group order; the automorphism-based 'graph multiplicity' correction for symmetric patterns appears only in later Zacros literature, not in this founding paper.
unverified.quote: Note that there are as many such mappings M (Eq. (15)) as lattice processes.

unverified.claim: Zacros prevents k-fold over-counting of symmetry-equivalent embeddings of the same pattern instance by design: for nonspecific sites its detection algorithms are restricted to returning only a single valid mapping per pattern instance, rather than enumerating all equivalent mappings and correcting afterwards.
unverified.quote: For nonspecific sites, our algorithms seek only one valid mapping to avoid unnecessary proliferation of interaction pattern instances.

unverified.claim: Erlebacher's atomistic dealloying KMC model uses site coordination-dependent rules for both processes: surface diffusion of all alloy components and dissolution of the less-noble atoms are each governed by the local coordination number of a site.
unverified.quote: a kinetic Monte Carlo model incorporating site coordination-dependent surface diffusion of all alloy components, and site coordination-dependent dissolution of the less-noble atoms

unverified.claim: Because event patterns carry no positional data and are detected purely by graph matching, the framework does not require enumerating multiple orientations of a reaction pattern (unlike earlier lattice-KMC codes such as CARLOS) — any lattice embedding with the same neighboring structure is detected as the same elementary step, which is precisely the guarantee an anchored point-group minimization lacks.
unverified.quote: For our purposes, no position data are required for the sites of the elementary reaction graphs. Thus, one does not need to define multiple orientations for a reaction pattern as done in previous KMC frameworks (for instance in the CARLOS code); as long as the neighboring of the entities on the lattice is similar to that of the elementary reaction pattern, the latter will be detected as a legitimate lattice process.

unverified.claim: In-plane vacancy hops within the surface layer are not chemically equivalent to each other: an in-plane hop is energetically unfavorable specifically when it would place the vacancy directly above a subsurface Cr atom, meaning in-plane vs inter-layer <110> hop distinction near the surface additionally depends on sub-layer chemical environment.
unverified.quote: When a Cr atom sits in the atomic plane just below the free surface, any in-plane vacancy hopping jump that would result in the vacancy sitting on top a subsurface Cr atom is energetically unfavorable.
